Outline ▶We will see two Combinatorial Optimization problems: ▶The Traveling Salesman Problem. ▶The Matching Problem. ▶We will see their similarities and differences. ▶We will understand the size of a problem and the running time of an algorithm.

Oil company problem ▶Oil company. ▶47 drilling platforms. ▶Each platform has a set of controls to regulate rate of flow. ▶Periodically it is necessary to visit certain platforms to regulate rates of flows. ▶Traveling is done by helicopter, which leaves from and returns to the helicopter base. ▶Oil company wants a method for routing the helicopter in such a way that the required platforms are visited, and the total flying time is minimized. ▶We assume that the flying time is proportional to the distance traveled.

Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) Euclidean TSP ▶Input: a set V of points in the Euclidean plane: V = {(xi, yi) : i = 1, . . . , n}. ▶Distance between (xi, yi) and (xj, yj) is √ (xi −xj)2 + (yi −yj)2. ▶Objective: find a tour passing through each point of V, for which the sum of the distances is minimized. ▶V consists of the platforms to be visited, plus the helicopter base. ▶Is it profitable to pass through a platform more than once?

Circuit drawing problem ▶Uses a plotter to draw a logic circuit ▶Plotter operates by moving a pen back and forth, and simultaneously rolling a sheet of paper forward and backwards ▶At the end, the pen should return to the starting position ▶The problem is to minimize the time required to draw the figure: ▶“pen-down” time, when actually drawing + ▶“pen-up” time, when the pen is not contacting the paper, ▶Question: Is it profitable, during “pen-down” time, to draw a line twice?
Circuit drawing problem ▶Pen-down time is fixed, but we can reduce the pen-up time. ▶Some amount of pen-up motion is necessary. Question: Why?

Circuit drawing problem ▶A node is a point of the figure from which a positive number of lines, other than 2, emanates. ▶A node is odd if there is an odd number of lines coming out, and even otherwise.

Circuit drawing problem Theorem The figure can be drawn, returning to the starting point, without tracing the same line twice and with no pen-up motion if and only if it is connected and there are no odd nodes.

Euclidean matching problem Euclidean matching problem ▶Input: a set V of points in the Euclidean plane, |V| even. ▶Objective: find a set of lines, such that each point is an end of exactly one line, and such that the sum of the lengths of the lines is minimized.

Similarities and differences Similarities: ▶Selecting sets of lines connecting points in the plane. ▶The number of feasible solutions is far too large to consider them all in a reasonable amount of time. ▶Most simple heuristics for the problems do not perform very well. Major difference: ▶There exists an eﬀicient algorithm for the Euclidean matching problem. ▶No such algorithm is known for the Euclidean TSP, and most researchers believe that no such algorithm exists. ▶If there would exist an eﬀicient algorithm for Euclidean TSP, then there would also exist an eﬀicient algorithm for about every combinatorial optimization problem.

Measuring running times ▶What is an “eﬀicient” algorithm? ▶We estimate the eﬀiciency by giving an upper bound on the number of steps it requires to solve a problem of a given size. ▶This only provides an estimate of an algorithm’s eﬀiciency (because the bounds are taken over all possible instances of a given problem). ▶Having a better bound does not necessarily mean better performance in practice. ▶We count the number of “elementary” operations in the execution of the algorithm: read, write, addition, multiplication, division, comparison.

Size of a problem ▶A combinatorial optimization problem consists of a discrete structure, together with a set of numbers. ▶The size of such a problem is the length of an encoding of the structure plus the cardinality of the set of numbers used. ▶Given an instance of a problem, let s be its size. We can say “the number of steps is bounded by 5s2 + 3s”.

We can say “the number of steps is bounded by 5s2 + 3s”. Example: ▶An instance of the Euclidean TSP can be specified by giving the (xi, yi) coordinates of the n points to be visited. ▶So the size of an instance is s = 2n.

Magnitude of the bound ▶We are interested in the performance on instances of large size. ▶We concentrate on the magnitude of the bound: 5s2 + 3s is “order s2”. ▶Formally: if f(s) and g(s) are positive real-valued functions on the set of nonnegative integers, we say f(s) ∈O(g(s)) if there exists a constant c > 0 such that f(s) ≤c · g(s) for all large enough values of s. Examples: 5s2 + 3s ∈O(s2) and 35 · 2s + s3 ∈O(2s). ▶Efficient algorithms are the ones that have running-time bounds of O(sk), for some k ∈N. ▶These algorithms are called polynomial-time algorithms, and their running times does not increase too rapidly as the problem size increases.

Example: Nearest Neighbor Algorithm for TSP ▶Initialization: initialize one object with three fields per point (xi, yi, mark = 0). 3n steps ▶Pass n −1 times : take a point vj, scan through all other objects (at most n −1 times ). For each object: ▶Check if the mark is equal to 0. (1 compare = 1 step ) ▶Compute the distance2 to vj and store it. (3 additions + 2 multiplications + 1 write = 6 steps ) ▶Keep track of the point vi∗that has the least distance2. (1 comparison + 1 write = 2 steps ) Then output vi∗as the next point in the tour 1 step , set vi∗’s mark field to 1 1 step and continue the search from vi∗. At most 3n + (n −1)((n −1) · 9 + 2) steps ∈O(n2).

Reduction to MST problem ▶So an optimal solution to the connector problem will not have any circuits. ▶A graph having no circuit is called a forest; a connected forest is called a tree. ▶We can solve the connector problem by solving the following: Minimum spanning tree (MST) problem Given a connected graph G and a real cost ce, ∀e ∈E, find a minimum cost spanning tree of G. ▶Connector problem and MST problem are equivalent for positive edge costs. ▶We solve the MST problem for arbitrary edge-costs.

The Augmenting Path Algorithm ▶Beginning with x = 0, repeatedly find an x-augmenting path P and augment x by the maximum value permitted. ▶This value is ϵ := min(ϵ1, ϵ2), where ϵ1 := min{ue −xe : e forward in P}, ϵ2 := min{xe : e reverse in P}. We call ϵ the x-width of P. ▶If such a path with x-width ∞is found, then there is no maximum flow, and the algorithm terminates. ▶If there is no x-augmenting path, then by Theorem 3.6 x is a maximum flow and the set R of nodes reachable by an x-incrementing path from r determines a minimum cut; again, the algorithm terminates.
